new_leaves.label: Ancient Cypriot Pottery
new_leaves.defn: The pottery of ancient Cyprus from the Chalcolithic to the Cypro-Classical period: Red-on-White and Red Polished handmade wares of the Chalcolithic and Early–Middle Bronze Age, the Late Bronze Age Base Ring and White Slip wares exported across the Levant, and the Iron Age White Painted, Bichrome and Black-on-Red wares with free-field figural jugs and barrel-shaped jugs.

new_leaves.label: Ancient Cypriot Sculpture
new_leaves.defn: The sculpture of ancient Cyprus: Chalcolithic picrolite cruciform figurines, Bronze Age terracotta plank figures, and the limestone and terracotta votive statues dedicated in the island's sanctuaries from the Cypro-Archaic to the Hellenistic period, in a local style that absorbed Near Eastern, Egyptian and Greek forms.

new_leaves.label: Seljuk Stucco
new_leaves.defn: Carved, moulded and painted stucco of the Seljuk lands (11th–13th century): the stucco figures of courtiers, guards and rulers and the ornamented friezes that lined the inner walls of Seljuk palaces, with the stucco revetments of mosques and tombs.

new_leaves.label: Predynastic Egyptian Pottery
new_leaves.defn: The pottery of prehistoric Upper Egypt, c. 4400–3000 BCE, in Petrie's sequence: Badarian and Naqada black-topped red ware, the White Cross-lined ware of Naqada I, and the Decorated ware of Naqada II–III painted in red on buff marl clay with boats, figures and spirals, with the wavy-handled jars used to date the sequence.
new_leaves.aliases: Naqada pottery; Amratian pottery; Gerzean pottery

new_leaves.label: Paracas Pottery
new_leaves.defn: The pottery of the Paracas culture of the south coast of Peru (first millennium BCE): incised vessels painted after firing with resin-based colours, double-spout-and-bridge bottles and feline-face bottles, in geometric, zoomorphic and abstract designs; the forerunner of Nazca polychrome.

new_leaves.defn: Silver plate of the Byzantine Empire: domestic tableware with classical and biblical scenes (4th–7th century), church silver (chalices, patens, processional crosses) and the imperial control stamps that dated it; about 1,500 plates and crosses survive.

new_leaves.defn: The jewellery and amulets of pharaonic Egypt, in gold, silver, semi-precious stones and faience: scarabs and scaraboids, protective amulets of deities and symbols, broad collars, pectorals, rings, bracelets and bead jewellery. Faience as a material and its vessels are E2-15.

new_leaves.label: Pala Painting
new_leaves.defn: The manuscript painting of Bengal and Bihar under the Pala dynasty (c. 10th–12th century), the earliest surviving Indian book painting: small panels of Buddhist deities and scenes on the palm leaves and painted wooden covers of Buddhist texts, above all the Prajnaparamita; the style was carried on in Nepal and Tibet. The manuscripts as books are C2-5.

new_leaves.label: Classical Javanese Sculpture
new_leaves.defn: The Hindu and Buddhist sculpture of Java from the 8th to the 15th century, in stone and in bronze, silver and gold: the Central Javanese period of the Sailendra and Mataram kingdoms (Borobudur, Prambanan) and the East Javanese period of Singhasari and Majapahit (the Prajnaparamita of Java). The temples as buildings are K9-2.

new_leaves.label: Mamluk Pottery
new_leaves.defn: The pottery of the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and Syria (1250–1517): underglaze-painted fritware of Damascus and Cairo, often in blue and black on white after Chinese porcelain, and the incised and slip-painted sgraffito earthenware with heraldic blazons and inscriptions naming amirs.

new_leaves.defn: The court and luxury textiles of Mughal India (16th–18th century): silk and gold-thread brocades and velvets, embroidered and painted cottons, patka sashes and Kashmir-type shawls, with the flowering-plant designs of Shah Jahan's reign shared with every other Mughal medium. new_leaves.label: Ancient Greek Bronzes
new_leaves.defn: The bronze work of ancient Greece from the Geometric to the Hellenistic period, apart from monumental statuary (D5-57): votive figurines, tripods and cauldrons, hydriae, kraters and other vessels exported as far as the Celts (the Vix Krater), polished mirrors with caryatid handles and later folding mirrors, and armour.

new_leaves.label: Halaf Pottery
new_leaves.defn: The polychrome painted pottery of the Halaf culture of northern Mesopotamia and Syria (c. 6100–5100 BCE), fired in two-chambered kilns: thin-walled bowls and jars painted in red, black and white with bucrania, rosettes, Maltese squares and checker patterns.
new_leaves.see: E1 Samarra Ware; E1 Ubaid Pottery
catalogues: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search?q=Halaf

new_leaves.label: Ubaid Pottery
new_leaves.defn: The greenish-buff pottery of the Ubaid period of Mesopotamia (c. 5500–3700 BCE), painted in dark geometric designs and increasingly made on the slow wheel, spread from southern Iraq to the Gulf and Anatolia before the Uruk period.
new_leaves.see: E1 Samarra Ware; E1 Halaf Pottery
